Click it to see only its works in the pool. Select arrows show where a seed was chosen from; Cited by, Cites and Related arrows, the list a seed gave. Above, E3 was chosen from the pool, where it appears in both L1 and L2: it cites both seeds. Under the map, Layout: Landscape grows the map to the right, and Portrait grows it down, which shows more of a long search at once.

Every list pours into one Pool, each work once, ranked by Links, the number of seeds it cites or is cited by, then by Cited. A work that cites three of your seeds is more likely about your question than one that cites one, however cited. From names the lists a work is in, Show narrows the pool to All, one list, New Since Last Step, or Candidates, the works of the top 20 neither seeds nor excluded; Seed beside a work makes it a seed. Click Links, Year or Cited to sort by it, largest first; click again for smallest first. Sorted by Links, works tied on seeds come in order of their influential citations, the filled dots. Related lists, for each seed, the works Semantic Scholar recommends by the likeness of their titles and abstracts, mostly recent, up to 500; for a seed it has no record of, often an older one, the ten or so OpenAlex relates to it. They join the pool marked ≈, but a recommendation is not a citation: Links does not count them.

Add two to five seeds you trust: too few and the pool follows one author's network; too many and every step costs many requests. Click Cited By, for the works citing each seed, or Cites, for the works each seed cites. Each seed not followed so yet gives a list; a seed already followed is skipped. Read the top of the pool, and make seeds of the works that belong to your question, especially recent ones with several Links. Click Cited By or Cites again, and repeat. Clicking a seed on the map, or its E number in Seeds, chooses it: it is drawn filled, a note under the map names the seeds chosen, and Cited By, Cites and Related follow those alone. Click a chosen seed again to drop it, or All Seeds to follow all seeds again. The beside a seed removes it: it and its lists stay on the map, dashed, and Links no longer counts it.

The line above the pool reads, for instance, 286 works from L1–L2 · the last step added 166, 9 of them in the top 20. While a step still brings works into the top 20, the literature is still opening up. When a step adds few or none there, the search has converged: the central works are in the pool, and further steps bring only the periphery. The search goes in rounds: a round is the works made seeds, and the Cited By or Cites lists that follow them. After each round, the line below it compares the pool's top 20 with the round's before, for instance Round 3 (L5–L6, from E4, E5): 4 works new to the top 20, and marks those works ↑ New in the top 20. Make the best of them seeds and follow them. When a round brings nothing new into the top 20, the line reads The search has saturated: the stopping point the guidelines for systematic reviews call saturation. Related lists change no work's Links, so they count in no round. Run to Saturation runs the rounds for you. It follows the seeds not followed yet; then, each round, it makes the best candidates seeds and follows them, until a round brings nothing new into the top 20. Beside it, Seeds a round (5 unless you change it) sets how many candidates a round makes seeds, Rounds at most (6 unless you change it) when to stop if the search has not saturated, and Following whether by Cited By, Cites or both. Pollis remembers what you set. Stop ends the run once its round ends. The top ranks works by how central they are, not by whether they are on your question: Exclude beside a work keeps it out of the top, and so out of the candidates, and Include ranks it again.

Tick Ask Semantic Scholar About the Citations before Cited By or Cites. Each dot under Links is then a seed the work cites, or is cited by: filled when Semantic Scholar finds the citation influential, hollow otherwise. Click the dots for, seed by seed, why one cites the other (Background, Method or Result) and the sentences citing it. A work cited only in passing in the introduction is rarely a good seed; one that uses a seed's Method often is. No Semantic Scholar record leaves the ranking as it is.

Each step is kept in the map's record. Save... writes it to ~/.pollis/literature: a TOML file of the name you give, with the seeds and steps, and a DuckDB file beside it with the works found. Open... brings a saved map back; New Search starts again. OpenAlex has no record of E1 that Pollis could find & Its title or first author differ from OpenAlex's: add it from PollisReferences with its DOI. The works citing E1 are L1 already & Each seed is followed once: choose another seed, or make new ones. The free budget of OpenAlex … is used up for today & Try again tomorrow, or set a key in Discover Literature. Semantic Scholar could not be reached, or is too busy just now & Click the dots again later.

The four databases that come with Pollis: what each holds, and how to add journal metrics. Pollis makes four DuckDB databases the first time the Julia REPL starts (Getting Started, page 2), and keeps them in ~/.pollis/databases. All four are read-only: Pollis rebuilds them when what they come from changes, and your own tables go in a database of your own. In the Databases view each is marked built-in; clicking it connects it in the Julia REPL. The duckdb> terminal, the sql> mode and PollisDB.connect() attach all four (Data and Databases, page 6). Database In Julia What it holds PollisDatasets pollis The 57 datasets of PollisDatasets, a table each, with their descriptions. PollisRSS rss Every item of the feeds you follow, kept by month; empty until feeds are read (RSS Feeds, page 22). PollisJournals journals About 250,000 journals, conferences and book series, from OpenAlex; the Norwegian register's levels; and the journal metrics you import. PollisReferences references Every work Pollis cites, and those you save from Literature Radar (page 36) or add to a panel's Explore References, with abstracts, keywords and dated citation counts.

items One row per item: feed, topic, title, link, published, received, summary, picture and media. feeds One row per feed, with its topic and number of items. zotero The items added to Zotero, with the collection. episodes The podcast episodes downloaded, with the file.

journals One row per journal, conference or book series in OpenAlex: title, ISSNs, publisher, country, field, works, citations, 2-year mean citedness, h-index, open access and article charges. journal_years The works and citations of each journal, by year. journal_issns Every ISSN, print and electronic, with its journal's id. norwegian_register The 40,000 journals and series of the Norwegian register, with field, DOAJ and the journal_id of the journal in journals. norwegian_levels Their level each year since 2004: 0 not academic, 1 academic, 2 leading, X under review. metrics The journal metrics you import (below): title, category, ISSNs, year, source, then the metrics. journal_metrics The same, with the journal_id of the journal in journals, found by ISSN. articles The articles of email alerts and those saved from Literature Radar, with journal, citations, FWCI and percentile. OpenAlex's data are CC0, free for any use. The Norwegian register is under the Norwegian Licence for Open Government Data (NLOD) 2.0, distributed by HK-dir. PollisJournals.jl brings a new copy of both every month, and Pollis rebuilds the database when it is installed. metrics, journal_metrics and articles are views over your own files in ~/.pollis/journals: always current, and never replaced by an update.

all_references Every work once, with its key (Appendix: Reference Keys), type, authors, venue, DOI, abstract and keywords; origin is pollis, corrected (yours, over Pollis's) or user. all_counts Citation counts, each with its source and the date it was observed, never added up. all_versions The records of a work you saved in OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar: the article, a preprint, a working paper. user_panels The works you added to, or hid from, a panel's Explore References. Pollis's own (pollis_references, pollis_counts) come from PollisReferences.jl and are replaced at each update. Yours (user_references, user_counts, user_versions) are views over your files in ~/.pollis/references, never replaced. A work Pollis already has is not added again: it keeps Pollis's key, and only its versions and counts are yours.

Impact factors, quartiles and ratings are not free to share, so PollisJournals does not come with them: you bring your own, downloaded from their source, and Pollis adds them to the database. The Journal Metrics page (Explore > RSS > Journal Metrics, or right-click PollisJournals) has a card per source, with its download page, what you have imported and Remove; Ask an Agent starts your coding agent on the Journal Metrics skill, to help you choose, download and import. Source Metrics Where to get it SCImago Journal Rank SJR, its quartile, h-index Free: scimagojr.com, Download data, a year at a time CWTS Journal Indicators SNIP, IPP Free: journalindicators.com, one file with every year ABDC Journal Quality List A*, A, B, C (business and economics) Free: abdc.edu.au, the Excel file of the latest list Scopus CiteScore, its quartile Free with an Elsevier account: scopus.com/sources Journal Citation Reports JIF, 5-year JIF, JIF quartile, JCI With a Clarivate subscription, often through a university library Download the file, as CSV or Excel. On the Journal Metrics page, Import File...; or right-click PollisJournals and choose Import Journal Metrics.... Choose the file. Pollis tells the source by the file's columns, so you do not have to. The year comes from a column of the file, its headers or its name; when none has it, Pollis asks. Refresh PollisJournals: the rows are in metrics and journal_metrics. Each file imported becomes a file of Pollis's own in ~/.pollis/journals/metrics, which the two views read; the file you downloaded is no longer needed. Importing the same file again replaces its rows, and the metrics stay when Pollis or PollisJournals is updated. On the RSS Feeds page, the tags of journal items then show the SJR or Impact Factor quartile, and Journals offers SJR Q1, SJR Q1–Q2 and SNIP Above 1.

A journal's metrics from every source, newest first: SELECT year, source, sjr_quartile, snip, jif FROM journal_metrics WHERE title = 'Econometrica' ORDER BY year DESC The works you saved from Literature Radar, with their latest OpenAlex count: SELECT r.key, r.title, max_by(c.count, c.date) AS cited FROM PollisReferences.all_references r JOIN PollisReferences.all_counts c USING (key) WHERE r.origin = 'user' AND c.source = 'openalex' GROUP BY ALL Import Journal Metrics... is not in the menu & Right-click PollisJournals itself, not one of its tables, or use the Command Palette. Not a file Pollis can import & It reads the exports of the five sources above only. A file of an older edition may have other column names: Help > Report Issue. A row has no journal_id & No journal in OpenAlex has its ISSN, as for many book series and conference proceedings. Its metrics are still in the views. A journal has two rows for a year & One per source; SCImago also lists some journals twice, under an old and a new title.

How every work cited in Pollis is kept once, and how to write its key from the work in front of you. Pollis keeps rich references: besides its title, authors and venue, each work has, wherever they can be found, its abstract, its keywords and its citation counts over time, each marked with where it came from. Every article, book, report and package referenced in Pollis, by a panel, a notebook or a method, is kept once, in PollisReferences.jl, a package of its own. Panels, notebooks and methods name a work by its key only; the pollis.bib that reports cite from, and the references a panel shows, are built from it. A correction is therefore made in one place.

A key is the authors, the year and a letter: FF1993a (Fama and French, 1993), Bre2001a (Breiman, 2001). Anyone with the work in front of them can write everything up to the year; the letter is the database's. Authors The key starts with Example One The first three letters of the surname: a capital, then lower case. A shorter surname is used whole. Bre, Bol, Wu Two to five The initial of every surname, in the order of the work, not alphabetical. FF, TL More than five The first five initials, then ... ABCDE...2019a Some not found, after looking The initials of those known, then ...; one known author keeps the three letters. Never a shortcut: five known authors are five initials. AB...1975a, Rac...2020a An organisation The capitals of its name as printed, without Inc. or Ltd.; a one-word name that is not an acronym reads like a sole author. ECB, IMF, AV, EI, Kag None U, for unknown. U2026a

Always the last word of the surname: Lopez de Prado Pra; Puigdomènech Badia B; van Gogh and Van Gogh G; El Ghaoui G. A hyphenated surname is one word, read from its start: El-Ghaoui E; Rhys-Jones R; Ben-Tal B. As the work prints it. Accents are removed (Sánchez San, Øksendal Oks), and an apostrophe keeps the first letter (O'Neill O).

The year has four digits: 1924, 2024. A forthcoming work takes the year expected; an undated one, 0000. The letter is always there: a, then b, … z, then aa, ab, …, in the order the works are added. If FF1999a and FF1999b are taken, the next work of Fama and French from 1999 is FF1999c. A key is given once and never changes, even if the work's authors or year are later corrected.

Look the work up by its DOI and its title: it may be there already, perhaps under another spelling of a name (El Ghaoui, El-Ghaoui). Write the key up to the year, from the work itself. The database adds the letter, and lists the works already under the same authors and year. A package is cited by the paper it asks to be cited by, in its CITATION.bib or CITATION.cff; when there is none, by the package itself, with the authors it names.

references One row per work: its type (article, book, inproceedings, incollection, techreport, phdthesis, misc), title, authors, year, venue, volume, pages, DOI, arXiv and OpenAlex ids, links, a free full text when there is one, the abstract and the keywords, each with its source. A row is changed only to add what is missing or to correct a mistake. counts The citations of a work as a source reported them on a day: key, count, source and date. Rows are only added, so each source's counts can be followed over time. The type of a work is stated where it is added, never guessed from its venue. Abstracts come from the DOI's record, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar or arXiv, and a package's from its About text on GitHub. Keywords are OpenAlex's, which it assigns itself, arXiv's subject categories or a package's GitHub topics. Citation counts from OpenAlex and Crossref are added every month; Google Scholar has no interface for this, so its counts are entered by hand. The key you wrote is taken & Expected: the database gives the next letter. Check the works it lists under that key first: one may be the same work. A work is in twice & Its name was spelt two ways. Keep the older key, and correct the other's uses.
